questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070891/assets/8ba69d7bfe8dd363288bbf86661172004b21143f02c70260da0c184f066a7c12.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{3},\,y{e}^{y+1}+x⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{3})\,dx+(y{e}^{y+1}+x)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070891/assets/3b90abecc774b5ba5dcee19385fef38b14206d2c31c3b6cba38216bfa9957448.png)

Since $P(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=y{e}^{y+1}+x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{3})\,dx-(y{e}^{y+1}+x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,\pi \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-3\cdot {r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-3{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )r\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070891/assets/e44543ad51864a7db6b8e80b5c560a1ac773a7537573014f737451af4d1209a7.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}(x{y}^{2}-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx+(2{x}^{2}y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,dy\,?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070891/assets/d8ee02b2b7282349604dc6305c0b2be796cfdbd2937e06d089e660683a5785ad.png)

Since $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $Q(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy-\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4xy-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(x{y}^{2}-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx+(2{x}^{2}y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4xy-\operatorname{cos}⁡x-(2xy-\operatorname{cos}⁡x))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 5,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

 

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}2(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{5}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{5}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070891/assets/e49bde14ba6097dfc7b153d5b93c2be2462b141a37357bfff826c852fc1136eb.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}(2-xy+2{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+xy)\,dy\,?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070891/assets/8b3c794f11c0a9be558e66c1c7a4ae4cd996037bbd6e491eefaa1a2e9000c596.png)

Since $P(x,y)=2-xy+2{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-x+4y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x+y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(2-xy+2{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+xy)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y-(-x+4y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3x-3y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 8,\,-\pi \le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(3x-3y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(3r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{8}3{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Line Integral Using Green's Theorem
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070891/assets/d675e8d06f2037531a2eec3a7e48374bb0d2e5cb59adfee0cbee5ce3a23add67.png)

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y)dx+({e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070891/assets/96998e4a17d20459622486970518a677309b23fd936c993d8c97dcf0d65a9a29.png)

 

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)={e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2},
$$

 we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y)dx+({e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2{y}^{2}-(-2{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}2({r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}2{r}^{3}({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\frac{81}{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{2}[\theta ]_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{81}{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{81\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}(\sqrt{5+x}-3{x}^{2}y)dx+({e}^{-{y}^{2}}+3x{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070891/assets/6273034b38059d3d49b2a29c91052c290151b4a29073f1c925172dd1c4c2bf72.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)=\sqrt{5+x}-3{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)={e}^{-{y}^{2}}+3x{y}^{2},
$$

we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-3{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{5+x}-3{x}^{2}y)dx+({e}^{-{y}^{2}}+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{y}^{2}-(-3{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,2\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}3({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{4}3{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{4}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}60\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =180[\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =180\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =90\pi \end{aligned}
$$
